title: Compact credential priming and fluent pullstream APIs across Python/TypeScript/Go
author: Maya Chen
commits: a3f2d1e feat(python): add credential priming facade and background warmup
b4c9e7a feat(ts): implement fluent pullstream consumer facade
c1d9f90 feat(go): lightweight pullstream adapter and opt-in priming hook
d7a8b33 refactor(shared): move priming policy to shared credentials package
e9b4c12 test: add integration smoke tests and cross-sdk fixtures
f0e4a55 docs: migration guide and examples
description:
Motivation: SDK consumers repeatedly asked for smaller, deterministic integration points for auth warmup and easier streaming consumption patterns. Current SDKs have similar behaviors implemented ad-hoc per-language; this PR unifies the core primitives and surfaces ergonomic facades in each SDK so teams can opt-in to credential priming and a fluent pullstream API without large surface changes.

Summary: This change introduces a compact credential priming policy in the shared SDK surface and language-specific ergonomic wrappers: a small Python priming facade that starts background token warmup, a TypeScript fluent pullstream consumer that turns the async iterator into a chainable DSL, and a Go adapter that provides a low-alloc pullstream handle plus an opt-in priming hook. The PR also adds cross-sdk deterministic retry matrices documentation and a short migration guide.

What I changed (high level):
- Extracted priming logic into sdks/shared/credentials/priming_policy.go and exposed a minimal API used by each SDK.
- Python: sdks/python/redwood/session/priming.py — session.priming.start(prime_before=30s) and a background worker with bounded concurrency.
- TypeScript: sdks/typescript/src/pullstream/fluent.ts — fluent .map/.filter/.batch chainable helpers and a small adapter to convert existing async iterables.
- Go: sdks/go/pullstream/adapter.go — pullstream.Handle and an OptInPriming(ctx) helper to reduce allocations in high-throughput servers.
- Tests: integration and unit tests added for priming behavior and pullstream ergonomics.
- Docs: migration guide and examples for each SDK.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc reviewed with SDK leads (ENG-4952)
- [x] Shared priming policy implemented and covered by unit tests
- [x] Language wrappers implemented and smoke-tested against staging backends
- [x] Changelogs and migration notes added
- [x] CI pipeline green after rerun

Compatibility notes: The priming API is opt-in; no breaking changes to existing public SDK surface are made by default. The new fluent pullstream is additive — consumers can migrate gradually. The shared deterministic retry matrix is documentation-only for now; follow-up PRs will wire it into client-side presets.

Benchmark & safety: Microbenchmarks show <3% latency increase at cold start for priming enabled workloads but >15% tail reduction for sustained streaming scenarios where token refresh races previously occurred. Priming defaults are conservative (disabled) and limited to the session object to avoid unexpected network traffic.

Testing/CI: All language pipelines run; intermittent flaky test in TypeScript pullstream suite was addressed by adding a short jitter in test harness. The CI run associated with this PR passed on the second attempt (flaky e2e rerun).

Review summary: See review conversation below for requested changes and responses.

Merge: squashed and merged into main on 2026-02-26. Release notes appended to SDK CHANGELOGs.

Notes for maintainers: follow-up tasks include wiring deterministic retry presets into SDK constructors (ENG-4988) and adding telemetry for priming hits/misses to the Console observability surface.
review_comments: Arjun Patel: Please clarify thread-safety of the Python priming worker and ensure it cannot spawn unbounded greenlets in ASGI environments. (requested changes)
Maya Chen: Addressed — worker now uses an explicit concurrency semaphore and ties lifecycle to session.close(). Added tests for asyncio/gunicorn interop.
Sofia Reyes: TypeScript fluent API looks ergonomic, can we preserve backward-compatibility for existing iterator consumers? (comment)
Maya Chen: The fluent facade accepts any AsyncIterable and returns an object exposing .toAsyncIterator() so existing code paths continue to work. Added example in docs. (resolved)
Liam O'Connor: Go adapter allocates on hot path; suggest pool reuse for handles. (requested changes)
Maya Chen: Implemented a small sync.Pool in adapter.go and added benchmark; allocation tail dropped ~40%. (resolved)
QA: Found intermittent failure in e2e CI for ts-pullstream—added 50–150ms jitter in test harness to stabilize.
